Send draft POC plan with milestones, success criteria, and pricing by Fri Aug 8

summary: POC scoping focused on integrating DataVista's inference scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness, defining success criteria (latency/throughput/cost/quality), load testing plan (streaming vs non-streaming), and a two-week timeline for baseline and stress tests.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-06 14:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (DataVista Eng Manager), Priya Singh (DataVista ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (DataVista SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um yeah I'm Jordan Park from Redwood Inference, I'm the AE on this one — with me is Maya Chen, our systems engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Tom: good, thanks. quick note we have Priya and Liam on from our side. looking forward to scoping this POC.
[00:12] Maya: awesome, quick agenda: align on success criteria, review your current scripts and workload, talk about harness integration, streaming versus non‑streaming tests, and define timeline and next steps. sound good?
[00:22] Priya: yeah that's perfect.
[00:24] Liam: yup.
[00:26] Jordan: ok first — Tom could you give a quick overview of what you're trying to validate in the POC, the must‑haves?
[00:31] Tom: sure, uh our main goal is twofold: 1) make sure Redwood's serving can handle our real inference mix at scale — we have a mix of short chat prompts and longer document summarization, and 2) ensure latency and cost meet our targets. specifically we want p50 latency < 150‑200ms for short chat token outputs and p95 under 700ms for interactive flows. for batch long runs we're ok with higher tail. also security — we need VPC/private deployment constraints validated.
[01:05] Jordan: great. those are reasonable. Maya, from a harness perspective, we typically capture both streaming and non‑streaming modes. we can run prefix caching tests, KV cache reuse, and measure tokens/sec and latency distribution.
[01:18] Maya: yes, and we have an existing benchmark harness repo that we share — it has a pluggable adapter so you can drop in customer scripts. Jordan will send the link after. the harness supports two modes: streaming (server sends partial tokens) and non‑streaming (waits until full response). each has different implications for concurrency and observed latency.
[01:36] Priya: quick question — our current inference script uses a custom batching layer and streams token deltas to the client; we worry that streaming tests will be noisy if the harness doesn't match our batching. can you mimic our batching layer?
[01:50] Maya: yeah that's what the adapters are for. if you give us your script and the sample payloads, we can write a thin adapter that calls your batching API. we typically ask for a canonical runner and an example set of requests.
[02:05] Priya: ok we'll share that.
[02:07] Jordan: on success criteria — beyond latency p50/p95 we should include throughput (concurrent request count and tokens/sec), cost per 1M tokens estimate for each model profile, and a quality regression check (we'll run a small eval set to compare outputs). how does that map to your stakeholders?
[02:22] Tom: that's good. product cares about latencies and p50 for chat, infra cares about tokens/sec and tail latencies, finance wants cost envelope. quality is critical — if outputs degrade we can't roll forward.
[02:33] Liam: also add network egress and VPC peering timing — we need to schedule a maintenance window for peering tests.
[02:40] Jordan: noted.

[02:42] --- Topics: workload sizing ---
[02:45] Maya: let's talk numbers. from the notes you shared earlier, Priya, you expected steady 200 RPS of short chat (avg 40 tokens output) and about 20 concurrent long summarization jobs (avg 1,200 tokens). is that correct?
[02:58] Priya: yes that's the production mix during peak. the short chat is ~80% of interactions.
[03:04] Maya: ok for the harness we'll generate a workload mix: 80% short prompts, 20% long batches. for short chat we'll test targets at 100, 200, 400 RPS to find the knee. for long jobs we'll run concurrent workers at 10, 20, 40 to measure throughput and GPU utilization.
[03:20] Tom: do you simulate user think time? we have some variance.
[03:24] Maya: yes, harness supports think‑time distributions; we'll use your trace if you have it, otherwise default 250‑750ms.

[03:30] --- Topics: streaming vs non‑streaming ---
[03:32] Priya: how do you measure latency in streaming mode? is it first‑token latency or time to last token?
[03:37] Maya: both. streaming tests report first_token latency (time until first partial chunk) and full_response latency (time to final token). for user experience p50 first_token < 120ms is a common goal, but depends on model. we also track tokens/sec inbound/outbound.
[03:52] Priya: makes sense. for our UI, first token matters a lot.
[03:55] Jordan: note that streaming can mask per‑token compute cost; we capture cumulative cost and compare to non‑streaming runs. sometimes non‑streaming yields better aggregate throughput for long documents because of batching.

[04:08] Liam: what's your suggested test order? baseline non‑streaming to establish throughput, then streaming to validate UX?
[04:14] Maya: yes, baseline non‑streaming to profile kernel selection and GPU utilization, then streaming to measure first‑token latency and network patterns. we also run prefix caching scenarios that reuse KV caches across similar prompts to see hit rates.

[04:27] --- Topics: harness integration details ---
[04:30] Maya: integration steps: 1) you hand us a canonical runner script (python/node) and sample payloads, 2) we write a small adapter in the harness that invokes your runner, 3) we define workload profiles (RPS, concurrency, prompt distributions), 4) dry run to validate correctness, 5) full stress runs.
[04:48] Priya: our runner is a thin wrapper around our internal batching service; it's dockerized. is that ok?
[04:52] Maya: perfect — a docker entrypoint is one of our supported adapters. we can run the container in the harness agents.
[04:58] Tom: will you run the harness in our VPC or in Redwood's test accounts?
[05:02] Jordan: two options: hosted harness in Redwood test account (fastest) or we can run the harness in your VPC via a short‑lived agent for network parity. for security and realistic network characteristics we'd recommend running at least the load generator in your VPC or a peered environment.
[05:18] Liam: we'll prefer VPC peering so the path matches prod. what's required for peering?
[05:22] Jordan: we'll send a runbook but generally you'll open a cidr for our test agent, and we coordinate a window. Maya will follow up.

[05:30] --- discussion: metrics and dashboards ---
[05:33] Maya: the harness will push metrics to a temporary dashboard: tokens/sec, p50/p90/p95 for first token and full response, GPU utilization, memory, and cost estimates. we'll provide raw CSV/JSON for post‑hoc analysis too.
[05:47] Priya: can we also get per‑prompt latencies and classification if outputs diverge from baseline?
[05:52] Maya: yes, we can mark a golden eval set and surface text diffs and a small quality metric (BLEU/ROUGE or custom scoring you provide). that's how we watch for regressions during quantization or model swaps.

[06:05] --- conversation about timeline and success criteria ---
[06:08] Jordan: propose a two‑week POC: week 1 baseline and harness integration, week 2 stress tests, regression checks, and review. milestone 1: harness adapter and baseline results; milestone 2: high‑load runs and cost/quality report.
[06:21] Tom: two weeks sounds reasonable. finance wants an initial cost estimate before committing; can you provide estimated cost for 1M tokens at the configs we test?
[06:29] Jordan: yes we'll include cost estimates per profile and per model. note these are estimates — we'll show both hosted and dedicated capacity compares.
[06:36] Priya: what about model variants — do you recommend trying quantized models for cost?
[06:40] Maya: absolutely — we can test FP16/INT8 profiles where supported. we'll include quality regressions check so you can see delta in outputs. sometimes INT8 gives big cost wins with very small quality change.

[06:53] Liam: any concerns about stability with continuous batching? our batching behavior is a bit non‑standard.
[06:58] Maya: we can instrument that — we might ask you to run a few longer soak tests to ensure the runtime's KV cache and batching plumbing behaves under steady load.

[07:06] --- Questions from customer ---
[07:08] Tom: will we get artifacts and raw logs?
[07:10] Jordan: yes, full logs, CSV exports, and a final report. also we'll share the harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmark-harness (placeholder link) and a runbook doc.
[07:21] Priya: can we trigger tests ourselves or must Redwood run them?
[07:24] Maya: both. we can run tests for you and we'll also set up a self‑serve harness agent in your environment so your team can re‑run with modified payloads.

[07:33] --- small transcription glitch / crosstalk ---
[07:35] Tom: (overlapping) ok cool, uh —
[07:36] Priya: sorry, I was going to say we have some prompt templates that include tool calls; will the harness support tool‑calling/structured output?
[07:44] Maya: yes, we support function/tool calling flows; for structured output we capture the JSON blobs and diff them as well. sometimes the transcript may show 'Redwood Dedicate' instead of 'Redwood Dedicated' — fyi transcription quirk.

[07:58] --- deeper technical dive (Maya leads) ---
[08:00] Maya: on the SE side, important knobs: batching window, max batch size, KV cache shard size, and kernel selection for long sequences. we will collect sequence length distribution and recommend kernel/quant profiles. for long docs we may switch tiling kernels to avoid O(N^2) blowups.
[08:20] Priya: do you expose configuration for kernel selection and can we pin model versions?
[08:24] Maya: yes you can pin model versions and specific runtime profiles. we usually recommend starting conservative and then optimize.

[08:30] Jordan: for the tests we'll propose three model profiles: baseline (FP16), cost‑optimized (INT8/quantized), and a high‑throughput variant (pruned or smaller model). we'll compare latency, throughput, and quality across them.

[08:45] Liam: when you say 'cost estimates' — do these include infra reservation differences for Dedicated?
[08:48] Jordan: yes, we'll show a hosted per‑token cost estimate and an equivalent cost for dedicated reserved capacity using expected utilization assumptions.

[09:00] --- discussion: failure modes and fallbacks ---
[09:02] Maya: we'll also run fallback scenarios — saturating capacity to see how the smart routing responds, and model fallback to a smaller model to evaluate graceful degradation. do you want automatic fallback behavior enabled in the POC?
[09:15] Tom: yes we want to see both manual and automated fallback so product understands impact on latency and quality.

[09:22] Priya: any security hoops for running in our VPC? SSO, audit logs, KMS?
[09:27] Jordan: we support VPC private agents, SAML SSO, and KMS integrations; for the POC we'll enable audit logging and provide a temp key management runbook. full compliance (SOC2/ISO) docs we'll attach with the follow‑up.

[09:42] --- scheduling and logistics ---
[09:44] Maya: propose next week run: Mon‑Wed adapter and baseline, Thu stress runs, Fri analysis; we'll need the scripts no later than Aug 10 to hit the schedule.
[09:56] Tom: we can deliver scripts by Aug 10. Liam will coordinate peering window on Aug 9.

[10:02] Jordan: recap of next steps: Jordan to share harness repo and POC plan, Maya to prepare baseline config, DataVista to provide runner and payloads, Liam to confirm peering. we'll schedule the 90‑minute throughput window on Aug 12.
[10:17] Priya: sounds good.
[10:18] Tom: thanks everyone.
[10:19] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up with materials and the action items.

[10:25] --- end of meeting notes (transcription includes a few mis‑transcribed product names and occasional filler words)

Notes on content fidelity: transcription imperfect: e.g., 'Redwood Dedicate' appears once, 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash' in raw exports. Speaker labels approximate.
